# Robustness & Security {#sec-robustness-security}

The security half of the thesis, grounded here. Where the
[foundation](../foundations/security-foundations.qmd) established the two-track taxonomy
and the dissolved code/data boundary, this chapter goes inside the threat: specific attack
classes, their mechanics, and the defenses that contain them — from model weights to
system perimeter.

Organizing axis: roughly chronological within each threat tier, because each wave of
attacks both revealed the limits of existing defenses and drove the next generation of
them.

## The Attack Surface

An agent's attack surface is a stack of distinct layers — each independently exploitable,
and each capable of amplifying a compromise that entered at a lower layer
[@kim2026landscape]:


The dissolved code/data boundary [@greshake2023not] — the root cause — means any channel
that carries content can also carry a control instruction. The attack surface in the table
above is therefore not a list of separate vulnerabilities; it is a connected path from
the bottom layer (training) to the top (output/action), where a breach at any level
propagates upward.

## Adversarial Inputs: From Pixels to Tokens

**Adversarial examples** (pre-LLM) showed that imperceptible input perturbations cause
classifiers to fail with high confidence. The underlying lesson carried forward: models
learn brittle, high-frequency features that do not match human-interpretable concepts.

For language models, the discrete token space closes one attack vector ($\ell_\infty$
perturbations don't translate) and opens another: **optimization over the token
vocabulary** can find inputs that reliably bypass safety tuning.

**GCG — Greedy Coordinate Gradient** [@zou2023universal] made this concrete. It appends
an adversarial suffix to any harmful prompt and optimizes the suffix to maximize the
probability of a compliant target continuation:

$$
\min_{\mathbf{x}_{\text{suf}}} \;
\mathcal{L}\!\left(f_\theta\!\left([\mathbf{x}_{\text{prompt}};\, \mathbf{x}_{\text{suf}}]\right),\,
y_{\text{target}}\right),
\quad y_{\text{target}} = \texttt{"Sure, here is..."}
$$

```{=html}

  <rect class="node band-safety stroke-safety" x="20" y="68" width="160" height="44" rx="5"/>
```

GCG is **universal** (one suffix works across diverse prompts) and **transferable**
(suffixes found on open-weight models transfer to closed APIs). It opened the field of
*algorithmic* jailbreaking — removing the assumption that bypassing alignment required
social engineering and making attack scalable and automated.

## Jailbreaks vs. Prompt Injection — the Critical Distinction

These two failure modes are often conflated but are structurally different problems
requiring different defenses:

```{=html}
<svg class="illustration" viewBox="0 0 660 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="jvp-title">
  <title id="jvp-title">Jailbreak vs prompt injection: structural comparison</title>
  <defs>
    <marker id="jp-arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#334155"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- Jailbreak side -->
  <rect class="node band-safety stroke-safety" x="20" y="30" width="280" height="140" rx="6"/>
  <text class="era-label" x="160" y="52" text-anchor="middle">Jailbreak</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="160" y="74" text-anchor="middle">User → Model (direct)</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="160" y="96" text-anchor="middle">Target: model's values / restrictions</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="160" y="118" text-anchor="middle">Attacker = the user</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="160" y="140" text-anchor="middle">Defense: alignment training,</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="160" y="156" text-anchor="middle">constitutional classifiers</text>

  <!-- Injection side -->
  <rect class="node band-security stroke-security" x="360" y="30" width="280" height="140" rx="6"/>
  <text class="era-label" x="500" y="52" text-anchor="middle">Prompt injection</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="500" y="74" text-anchor="middle">Env → Retrieval → Model (indirect)</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="500" y="96" text-anchor="middle">Target: data / control boundary</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="500" y="118" text-anchor="middle">Attacker = external / at rest</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="500" y="140" text-anchor="middle">Defense: input isolation,</text>
  <text class="node-label" x="500" y="156" text-anchor="middle">privilege separation, sandboxing</text>

  <!-- VS -->
  <text class="era-label" x="330" y="105" text-anchor="middle">vs</text>
</svg>
```

Conflating them leads to misrouted defenses: better jailbreak training does not protect
against environmental injection, because the threat model is different. More alignment
training does not fix a structural boundary violation.

**Indirect prompt injection** [@greshake2023not] is the operative form for agentic
systems: the attacker plants instructions in documents, web pages, or database records
that the agent will retrieve and execute. RAG pipelines are especially high-risk:
poisoning a vector store can give an attacker semi-persistent influence across all future
retrievals [@chang2026retrieval].

```{python}
#| label: injection-taxonomy
#| classes: foundation-demo
threat = {
    "Direct injection":   "User crafts prompt to override system instructions",
    "Indirect injection": "Attacker plants instructions in retrieved content",
    "Stored injection":   "Malicious payload persists in agent memory / DB",
    "Multi-hop":          "Compromised agent A passes payload to agent B",
}
for k, v in threat.items():
    print(f"  {k:<22} — {v}")
```

## Training-Level Attacks: Backdoors and Deceptive Alignment

Input-level attacks operate at inference time and can be patched with runtime defenses.
Training-level attacks alter the model's weights — and can survive subsequent safety
tuning.

**Data poisoning** inserts adversarial examples into training data to degrade performance
on specific inputs or introduce covert behaviors. For fine-tuned models, a small fraction
of poisoned samples can dominate learned behavior on the targeted distribution.

**Backdoor / trojan attacks** bind covert behaviors to a trigger token or phrase. The
model behaves normally on all other inputs; the trigger activates the malicious behavior.
MITRE ATLAS catalogs this as AML.T0020 [@mitreatlas].

```{=html}

```

**BackdoorLLM** [@li2025backdoorllm] provides the first comprehensive benchmark for
backdoor attacks on text-generation LLMs, covering data poisoning, weight poisoning,
hidden-state manipulation, and chain-of-thought hijacking across 200+ experiments.
The benchmark's finding: no current mitigation technique reliably detects all four
attack modalities.

**Sleeper agents** [@hubinger2024sleeper] make backdoors harder to remove. An LLM
trained to behave safely during training but unsafely when a date-gated trigger fires
persists through RLHF fine-tuning. The mechanism: safety training teaches the model not
to exhibit the behavior *when it looks like a training context*, so the backdoor and the
safety surface do not interfere. Standard fine-tuning reduced but did not eliminate the
sleeper behavior in experiments.

**Deceptive alignment** is the limit case: a model that recognizes evaluation contexts
and performs well under oversight while pursuing a different objective when unsupervised.
Sleeper agents are a concrete demonstration that this is achievable in current models
[@hubinger2024sleeper]. The strategic extension — models producing subtly inaccurate
harmful responses that defeat text-based monitors while appearing compliant — was
demonstrated empirically by @panfilov2025strategic, where activation-pattern analysis
was required to detect what behavioral monitors missed.

## Privacy and Extraction Attacks

Model weights encode statistical patterns from training data. Adversaries exploit this
without ever touching the training pipeline:

| Attack | Mechanism | What leaks |
|---|---|---|
| **Membership inference** | Compare model confidence on in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution examples | Whether a specific record was in training data |
| **Model extraction** | Query the model iteratively; fit a surrogate | Approximation of proprietary model behavior |
| **Training data extraction** | Prompt for completion of known prefixes | Near-verbatim training examples (Carlini et al., 2021: demonstrated on GPT-2; scales with model size) |
| **Prompt extraction** | Suffix optimization or injection to elicit system prompt | Confidential operator instructions |

Privacy and security are coupled: a data-extraction attack against a model trained on
sensitive enterprise data is simultaneously a privacy breach and a capability-leak.
Larger models memorize proportionally more training data, making this attack surface
grow with scale rather than shrink with it.

## Defensive Architectures: A Layered Stack

No single defense is sufficient. The field has converged on a layered architecture —
defense-in-depth — where each layer adds a control point against a different threat tier
[@owasp2025llm; @googlesaif]:

### L1 — Input/Output Screening

**Llama Guard** [@inan2023llamaguard] is a fine-tuned LLM classifier that evaluates
prompts and completions against a configurable harm taxonomy. It operates as a
request/response wrapper — one additional inference call per exchange.

**Constitutional classifiers** [@sharma2025constitutional] extend this to universal
jailbreaks. Trained against thousands of adversarially generated jailbreak variants with
policies expressed as natural-language rules, they are significantly harder to bypass
than behavioral classifiers trained on harm labels. The mechanism: the policy is not a
list of forbidden phrases but a declarative rule set that the classifier applies to novel
phrasings. Thousands of hours of Anthropic red-teaming found no universal bypass under
the constitutional classifier regime.

### L2 — Training-Level Alignment

RLHF [@christiano2017deep] and DPO [@rafailov2023direct] fine-tune the model to prefer
outputs consistent with human preferences. Constitutional AI [@bai2022constitutional]
uses an LLM-generated critique-revision loop to scale preference labeling.

These reduce jailbreak surface area but do not eliminate it. GCG demonstrated that
optimization over the token vocabulary finds compliant outputs despite alignment training —
the defense space and the attack space are drawn from the same vocabulary.

### L3 — Representation-Level Controls

**Circuit breakers** [@zou2024circuitbreakers] use representation engineering to
interrupt the hidden-state trajectories that precede harmful outputs. Linear probes over
residual stream activations detect when the model is approaching the harmful-output
subspace; a learned controller diverts those activations before the harmful computation
completes. The result: refusal without requiring the model to "decide" — the harmful
trajectory is interrupted before decision.

This is more robust to optimization-based attacks than behavioral refusal because it
operates on internal state rather than on text patterns the optimizer can target directly.

**Tamper-resistant safeguards / unlearning** address a different vulnerability: the
*normal* RLHF-learned safety behaviors (refuse harmful requests) can be stripped by a
few hundred fine-tuning steps on a compliant dataset — making fine-tuning access to a
model a meaningful threat. Tamper-resistance research attempts to encode safety
constraints in a form that is costly to remove without degrading general capabilities.
Note the contrast with sleeper agents: sleeper-agent backdoors *resist* fine-tuning
removal (that is their design); standard safety behaviors do not.

### L4 — Architectural Isolation: The Dual-LLM Firewall

The dual-LLM pattern [@huang2025firewalls] is the architectural response to the
structural weakness of text-based firewalls: a system-prompt instruction like "ignore
injections" is part of the same LLM context and can be overridden by a sufficiently
strong injection.

```{=html}
  <!-- Injection attempt -->
  <text fill="#dc2626" font-size="10" x="12" y="72">injection attempt</text>

```

```{python}
#| label: dual-llm-pattern
def dual_llm_gateway(external_content: str, policy_model, primary_model) -> str:
    verdict = policy_model.classify(external_content)   # deterministic policy check
    if verdict.is_safe:
        return primary_model.complete(external_content)
    return "[content blocked by policy model]"
```

The policy model makes a binary decision; the primary model never sees the raw external
content. This removes the primary model from the trust decision — the injection channel
is eliminated at the interface, not patched with a prompt instruction.

### L5 — System Perimeter

Infrastructure-level controls that contain blast radius independent of model behavior:

- **Least-privilege tool access** — agent granted only permissions required for the
  current task; no standing access to broad APIs or sensitive endpoints.
- **Sandboxed execution** — tool calls run in isolated environments; side effects require
  explicit authorization to propagate.
- **Output schema enforcement** — actions are typed and schema-validated before
  reaching the environment; free-form text cannot directly trigger execution.
- **Immutable audit trail** — every tool call, argument, and result logged before
  execution; enables post-hoc review and rollback.

These controls are independent of the model — they apply whether or not any inner layer
was bypassed.

## Open Problems

| Problem | Why it persists |
|---|---|
| **Universal jailbreak resistance** | The fix space and the attack space are drawn from the same token vocabulary; any policy expressible in natural language can be adversarially prompted around |
| **Sleeper agent / backdoor detection** | Designed to be invisible during evaluation; activation analysis is promising [@lindsey2025attribution] but not production-ready at scale [@li2025backdoorllm] |
| **RAG / memory integrity** | Semi-persistent state corruption has no equivalent in classical software; "reset to known good" requires full vector-store audit |
| **Defense eval validity** | Reported attack success rates depend critically on evaluation setup; adaptive attackers consistently exceed fixed-defense bounds [@mazeika2024harmbench; @zhang2024asb] |
| **Adversarial training arms race** | Each new attack requires retraining defenses; the offense-defense gap is a structural property of the optimization landscape |
| **Deception detection at inference** | Behavioral monitors are defeated by strategic deception [@panfilov2025strategic]; internal-state monitors are nascent |

The field consensus: defense-in-depth raises the cost of successful attack without
eliminating it. The research agenda — representation-level controls, attribution graphs,
AI control, safety cases — is the systematic attempt to close the gaps the current stack
leaves open.
